100203.e: If you take frozen food out of the freezer, it gets warmer. The ice in it melts, and it defrosts.
100203.m: Frozen food defrosts in the warmth.

100204.q: What happens to a full glass bottle of water in the freezer?
100204.e: Water expands when it turns into ice. The ice needs more room and can break the bottle.

a: So that it goes mouldy faster
100205.e: In great cold, bacteria and mould can hardly grow. That is why food keeps for a long time in the freezer.
100205.m: Frozen food keeps for a long time.

100206.q: What builds up on the walls of the freezer over time?
100206.e: Moisture from the air freezes on the cold walls. This makes a layer of ice, which you defrost now and then.
100206.m: Ice builds up in a freezer over time.

100207.q: What should you do quickly after taking something out of the freezer?
100207.e: When the door is open, warm air flows in. Then the appliance has to use more electricity to get cold again.
100207.m: Close the freezer door again quickly.

100208.q: What must you not put in the freezer?
100208.e: Hot food warms up the freezer, and other things could start to thaw. Let it cool down first.
100208.m: Let warm food cool down before freezing it.

100209.q: What can happen if you touch an ice-cold ice lolly directly with your tongue?
a: Your tongue can stick to it.
100209.e: Very cold ice makes the spit on your tongue freeze instantly. Then your tongue sticks to it.
100209.m: Very cold ice can stick to your tongue.

100210.q: What gets hot on the cooker?
100210.e: The hotplate gets hot and passes the heat on to the pan. That is how the food is cooked.

100211.q: Why should you not touch a hotplate after cooking?
a: It stays hot for a long time.
100211.e: A hotplate stores heat. It stays hot for a while after being switched off.
100211.m: A hotplate stays hot after cooking.

100212.q: What do you need for an induction hob?
a: Pans with iron in the base
100212.e: An induction hob heats the base of the pan directly. This only works if the base contains iron.
100212.m: An induction hob needs magnetic pans.

100213.q: How can you test whether a pan works on induction?
100213.e: If a magnet sticks to the base of the pan, the pan works on an induction hob. If it does not stick, the pan will not get warm.
100213.m: A magnet shows whether a pan works on induction.

100214.q: What burns on a gas cooker?
100214.e: On a gas cooker, gas burns with a blue flame. The flame heats the pan.
100214.m: A gas cooker cooks with a flame.

100215.q: Which hotplate is best for a small pan?
100215.e: If the hotplate is bigger than the pan, heat is lost around it. With the right hotplate you save energy.
100215.m: The pan and the hotplate should be the same size.

100216.q: What is often built into a cooker under the hotplates?
100216.e: Many cookers have an oven built in underneath. You bake cakes or bread in it.
100216.m: There is often an oven under the hotplates.

100217.q: On many ceramic hobs, what does a glowing ‘H’ show?
100217.e: The ‘H’ is the residual heat indicator. It glows as long as the switched-off hotplate is still hot.
100217.m: An ‘H’ on the hob warns that a hotplate is hot.

100218.q: Which kernels are used to make popcorn?
100218.e: Popcorn is made from a special kind of maize called popping corn. Its kernels have a hard shell.

100219.q: Why does the maize kernel burst open?
a: The steam pushes the shell open.
100219.e: The steam inside the kernel has no room. At some point the pressure is so great that the hard shell bursts open.
100219.m: The steam in the kernel bursts the shell.

100220.q: Why do you put a lid on the pan when making popcorn?
100220.e: Bursting kernels jump up into the air. The lid stops them flying out of the pan.
100220.m: When making popcorn, put a lid on the pan.

100221.q: What colour is the inside of finished popcorn usually?
100221.e: The puffed-up inside of the maize kernel is white to light yellow. The brown shell stays on in small pieces.

100222.q: What is left if a maize kernel does not pop when you make popcorn?
100222.e: Some kernels have too little water or a damaged shell. They do not pop and stay hard.

100223.q: What do you often put in the pan before pouring in the maize kernels?
100223.e: The oil spreads the heat evenly around the kernels. That way they pop better and burn less.
100223.m: For popcorn you put a little oil in the pan.

100224.q: Why does food cook faster in a pressure cooker?
100224.e: In the closed pressure cooker, the pressure rises. Then the water only boils at higher temperatures, and the food cooks faster.
100224.m: In a pressure cooker it gets hotter than 100 degrees.

100225.q: What is special about the lid of a pressure cooker?
a: It just rests loosely on top.
100225.e: The lid is locked firmly and has a rubber seal. That way the steam cannot simply escape.
100225.m: A pressure cooker is sealed tight.

100226.q: What do you often hear when steam escapes from the valve of a pressure cooker?
100226.e: When there is too much steam in the pan, the valve lets some of it out. The steam rushes through the narrow opening and hisses.

100227.q: When may you open a pressure cooker?
a: When there is no pressure left inside
100227.e: If the pan is still under pressure, hot steam can shoot out. That is why you only open it once the pressure has gone.
100227.m: Only open a pressure cooker when there is no pressure.

100228.q: What shows that there is pressure in a pressure cooker?
100228.e: There is a valve on the lid. It rises when there is pressure in the pan and often shows rings.
100228.m: The valve shows the pressure in a pressure cooker.

100229.q: What do you save with a pressure cooker?
100229.e: Because the food is cooked faster, the cooker has to be on for less time. That saves time and energy.
100229.m: A pressure cooker saves time and energy.

100230.q: What is often cooked in a pressure cooker because it otherwise takes a long time?
100230.e: Potatoes take about 20 minutes or more in a normal pan. In a pressure cooker they are soft much sooner.
100230.m: Potatoes get soft faster in a pressure cooker.

100231.q: Why does a pressure cooker always need some water?
a: Without water there is no steam.
100231.e: The pressure in the pan comes from steam. Without water no steam is made, and the pan can be damaged.
100231.m: A pressure cooker always needs some water.

100232.q: What do you make from cream with a whisk?
100232.e: With a whisk you beat liquid cream until it becomes stiff. Then it is called whipped cream.
100232.m: You make whipped cream with a whisk.

100233.q: What do you beat into the cream with a whisk?
100233.e: The wires of the whisk whirl air into the cream. Lots of tiny air bubbles make it fluffy.
100233.m: A whisk beats air into cream.

100234.q: What do you get if you beat egg white with a whisk for a long time?
100234.e: When it is beaten, the egg white traps lots of air bubbles. It turns white and firm and becomes stiff egg whites.
100234.m: Beaten egg white becomes stiff and white.

100236.q: What happens if you whip cream for far too long?
100236.e: If you whip it too long, the fat in the cream clumps together. That makes butter.
100236.m: Cream whipped too long turns into butter.

100237.q: What material are the wires of a whisk usually made of?
100237.e: The wires are usually made of stainless steel. They are bendy, do not rust and are easy to clean.
100237.m: The wires of a whisk are usually metal.

100238.q: What is faster than a whisk used by hand?
100238.e: An electric hand mixer turns its beaters very fast. That way the cream gets stiff more quickly.
100238.m: Whipping is faster with a mixer.

100239.q: What should cream be like so that it whips well?
100239.e: Cold cream gets stiff faster when it is whipped. Warm cream hardly firms up, and frozen cream cannot be whipped at all.
100239.m: Cream whips best when well chilled.

100240.q: What do you need a pot holder for?
100240.e: A pot holder protects your hands from hot handles. That way you do not burn yourself.
100240.m: Use a pot holder to hold hot pans.

100241.q: Why does a thick pot holder protect well against heat?
a: It is as cold as ice.
100241.e: Fabric with lots of tiny air pockets only lets heat through slowly. That is why your hand hardly feels the heat.
100241.m: A thick pot holder hardly lets heat through.

100242.q: Why should a pot holder be dry?
a: A wet one conducts heat faster.
100242.e: Water conducts heat much better than dry fabric. You can burn yourself with a wet pot holder.
100242.m: A pot holder must be dry.

100243.q: What is a glove for taking hot trays out of the oven called?
100243.e: An oven glove is like a pot holder but protects your whole hand. You use it to take hot trays out of the oven.
100243.m: Use an oven glove to take hot trays out of the oven.

100244.q: What are pot holders often made of?
100244.e: Cotton is thick and soft and does not melt like some plastics. That is why many pot holders are made of cotton.
100244.m: Many pot holders are made of cotton.

100245.q: What is a small loop on a pot holder for?
100245.e: You use the loop to hang the pot holder on a hook. That way it is always to hand.
100245.m: You hang up a pot holder by its loop.

100246.q: What can you put a hot pan on so that the table is not damaged?
100246.e: A trivet protects the table from the heat. Without it, marks or burns could appear.
100246.m: Put hot pans on a trivet.

100247.q: Why should you never hold a pot holder close to an open flame?
100247.e: A pot holder is made of fabric and can burn. That is why you keep it away from flames.
100247.m: A pot holder can catch fire.

100248.q: What happens to ice cubes in a glass of water?
100248.e: Ice is lighter than the same amount of water. That is why ice cubes float on the surface.

100249.q: What can you put in the ice cube tray before freezing to make the ice cubes look pretty?
100249.e: If you put berries or mint leaves in the water, they freeze into the ice. That makes the ice cubes look lovely in a drink.
100249.m: Berries in ice cubes look pretty.

100250.q: What is it called when ice turns into water?
100250.e: When ice gets warm, it melts. Solid ice turns into liquid water.

100251.q: Why does a drink with ice cubes get cold?
a: The ice gives off cold like a cooker.
100251.e: Ice needs heat to melt. It takes this heat from the drink, so the drink gets cooler.
100251.m: Ice cubes take heat away from a drink.

100252.q: Where does an ice cube melt faster?
100252.e: Warm water gives a lot of heat to the ice. That is why it melts quickly there.
100252.m: Ice melts quickly in warm water.

100253.q: What can you see on the outside of a cold glass with ice cubes?
100253.e: The air contains water vapour. On the cold glass it turns back into water and forms drops.
100253.m: Drops form on the outside of a cold glass.

100254.q: What happens to the water level when ice cubes melt in the glass?
100254.e: A floating ice cube pushes aside as much water as it weighs. That is why the glass does not overflow when it melts.
100254.m: Melting ice cubes do not make a glass overflow.

100255.q: What shape is an ice cube usually?
100255.e: You pour water into a tray with small compartments and freeze it. The compartments are often cube-shaped.
100255.m: Ice cubes are usually shaped like a cube.

100256.q: What does a toaster do to bread?
a: It makes it brown and crispy.
It makes it soft and wet.
100256.e: In the toaster, the bread is heated from both sides. It turns brown and crispy.

100257.q: What glows red in a toaster?
100257.e: Electricity flows through thin wires and makes them very hot. They glow red and toast the bread.
100257.m: Heating wires glow in a toaster.

100258.q: What must you never put into a toaster that is switched on?
100258.e: Metal conducts electricity. If you reach into the toaster with a fork, you can get a dangerous electric shock.
100258.m: Never put metal into a toaster.

100259.q: What happens when the bread in the toaster is ready?
100259.e: In many toasters a spring pushes the bread up when the time is up. Then you can take it out.

100260.q: What happens if you toast bread for too long?
100260.e: With too much heat the bread burns. It turns black and tastes bitter.
100260.m: Bread toasted for too long burns.

100261.q: What do you set with the dial on a toaster?
100261.e: With the dial you set how long it toasts for. A longer time makes the bread darker.
100261.m: On a toaster you set how brown the bread gets.

100262.q: What collects at the bottom of the toaster?
100262.e: Small crumbs fall down while toasting. Empty the crumb tray now and then, when the toaster is off and cold.

100263.q: What do you put on top of some toasters to warm up bread rolls?
100263.e: Some toasters have a wire rack that fits on top. You put rolls on it, and the heat from below warms them up.
100263.m: With a bun warmer rack a toaster warms up rolls too.

100364.q: Roughly what share of the Earth's entire history does the Precambrian cover?
100364.e: The Precambrian stretches from the formation of the Earth about 4.6 billion years ago until about 540 million years ago. That is just over four billion years, almost nine tenths of the Earth's history.
100364.m: The Precambrian is by far the longest part of the Earth's history.

100365.q: Into which three eons is the Precambrian divided?
100365.e: The Hadean is followed by the Archean and the Proterozoic. The Palaeozoic, Mesozoic and Cenozoic, by contrast, are the eras of the younger eon, the Phanerozoic.
100365.m: The Precambrian consists of the Hadean, Archean and Proterozoic.

100366.q: After which figure from Greek mythology is the oldest eon of the Earth's history named?
a: After Hades, god of the underworld
100366.e: The Hadean is named after Hades because the young Earth, with its magma ocean and frequent impacts, was hellishly hot. It lasted until about 4 billion years ago.
100366.m: The Hadean bears the name of Hades, god of the underworld.

100367.q: Where were the oldest known minerals on Earth, zircon grains about 4.4 billion years old, found?
a: In the Jack Hills in Western Australia
In the Aar Massif in the Swiss Alps
In the Grand Canyon in Arizona
100367.e: Detrital zircons from the Jack Hills are up to about 4.4 billion years old. Zircon is very resistant and can be dated precisely with the uranium-lead method.
100367.m: The oldest mineral grains on Earth are zircons from Western Australia.

100368.q: Which rock in north-western Canada, at about 4 billion years, is one of the oldest reliably dated rocks on Earth?
100368.e: The Acasta Gneiss in the Canadian Shield has been dated to about 4.0 billion years. It therefore comes from the transition from the Hadean to the Archean.
100368.m: The Acasta Gneiss in Canada is one of the oldest rocks in the world.

100369.q: What is the youngest period of the Precambrian, named after hills in South Australia, called?
100369.e: The Ediacaran is named after the Ediacara Hills in South Australia and lasted from about 635 to 540 million years ago. In 2004 it was officially introduced as the first new period in over a hundred years.
100369.m: The Ediacaran is the last period before the Cambrian.

100370.q: What does the name Proterozoic literally mean?
100370.e: Greek “proteros” means earlier and “zoe” means life. “Old life” would be Palaeozoic, “middle” Mesozoic and “new” Cenozoic.
100370.m: Proterozoic means age of earlier life.

100371.q: In which eon do the first reliably proven cells with a nucleus (eukaryotes) appear?
100371.e: Fossils and chemical traces show eukaryotes reliably from the Proterozoic, about 1.6 to 2 billion years ago. According to current knowledge, only prokaryotes lived in the Archean.
100371.m: Cells with a nucleus have existed since the Proterozoic.

100372.q: What is the eon called in which the first continental cores formed and the oldest reliable traces of life appeared?
100372.e: The Archean lasted from about 4 to 2.5 billion years ago. During this time, cratons formed as stable continental cores, and the first microbial communities appeared.
100372.m: In the Archean the first continental cores grew.

100373.q: Why are animal fossils much more common from the Cambrian onwards than before?
a: Many animals formed hard shells and skeletons for the first time
Before that there was no water in the oceans yet
Older rocks were all destroyed by ice
Before that there were no sedimentary rocks at all
100373.e: With biomineralisation, armour, shells and spines of lime or phosphate appeared. Such hard parts are preserved as fossils much more easily than soft bodies.
100373.m: Hard shells made Cambrian animals easy to fossilise.

100374.q: Which naturalist saw the apparently sudden appearance of Cambrian fossils as a difficulty for his theory?
100374.e: In “On the Origin of Species”, Darwin wrote that the absence of older ancestors was hard to explain. He suspected gaps in the fossil record, which later finds from the Precambrian partly confirmed.
100374.m: Even Darwin was puzzled by the sudden appearance of Cambrian animals.

100375.q: In which country is the Chengjiang fossil site with superbly preserved early Cambrian animals?
100375.e: Chengjiang is in Yunnan province and is about 518 million years old. As in the Burgess Shale, soft parts are also preserved there.
100375.m: Chengjiang in China shows animals from the early Cambrian.

100376.q: Which animal with grasping head appendages is regarded as one of the largest predators of the Cambrian?
100376.e: Anomalocaris belonged to the radiodonts, early relatives of the arthropods. It caught other sea creatures with its grasping appendages.
100376.m: Anomalocaris was a large hunter in the seas of the Cambrian.

100377.q: Which environmental change is often named as a precondition for the Cambrian explosion?
a: A sharp fall in solar radiation
A reversal of the Earth's rotation
100377.e: Larger, active animals need more oxygen. Many researchers therefore see the rise in oxygen at the end of the Proterozoic as an important precondition.
100377.m: More oxygen made larger and more active animals possible.

100378.q: Which hypothesis explains the Cambrian explosion with the development of powerful eyes?
100378.e: The zoologist Andrew Parker suggests that eyes triggered an arms race between predators and prey. Armour, camouflage and fast movement would then be results of this.
100378.m: According to the Light Switch hypothesis, eyes triggered an evolutionary arms race.

100379.q: What is the group of multicellular organisms called that lived before the Cambrian explosion and mostly had no hard parts?
100379.e: The Ediacaran biota lived about 575 to 540 million years ago. Its organisms, often shaped like discs or fronds, are preserved only as imprints.
100379.m: The Ediacaran biota shows multicellular life even before the Cambrian.

100380.q: Roughly how long ago did the Great Oxidation Event begin?
100380.e: From about 2.4 billion years ago, free oxygen built up permanently in the atmosphere for the first time. This happened at the beginning of the Proterozoic.
100380.m: About 2.4 billion years ago, a lot of oxygen got into the air for the first time.

100381.q: Which living things triggered the Great Oxidation Event?
100381.e: Cyanobacteria were the first living things to carry out photosynthesis that releases oxygen. Over a long time, more and more oxygen got into the sea and the air in this way.
100381.m: Cyanobacteria filled the atmosphere with oxygen.

100382.q: Why was the rise in oxygen a catastrophe for many living things at the time?
a: Oxygen was poisonous to anaerobic organisms
Oxygen destroyed the Earth's magnetic field
100382.e: Most microbes were adapted to a life without oxygen. For them oxygen is strongly oxidising and harmful, so many were pushed back into niches without oxygen.
100382.m: For anaerobic microbes, oxygen was a poison.

100383.q: Which layered rocks formed when oxygen precipitated iron dissolved in the sea?
100383.e: Dissolved ferrous iron turned into insoluble iron oxide and settled as a layer. Alternating with layers of silica, this formed the banded iron formations, from which a lot of iron is extracted today.
100383.m: Banded iron formations are rust-red witnesses of early oxygen.

100384.q: What effect did the first big rise in oxygen probably have on the Earth's climate?
a: A very hot phase with over 50 °C
100384.e: Oxygen broke down the powerful greenhouse gas methane. About 2.4 billion years ago this was followed by the Huronian glaciation, one of the longest glaciations in the Earth's history.
100384.m: The Huronian glaciation accompanied the first big rise in oxygen.

100385.q: How could the rise in oxygen have cooled the climate greatly?
a: It broke down the greenhouse gas methane
It darkened the Sun with dust
It greatly increased the carbon dioxide content
100385.e: Oxygen oxidises methane into carbon dioxide and water. Because methane is a much stronger greenhouse gas, the greenhouse effect weakened.
100385.m: Less methane meant a cooler climate.

100386.q: By which other name is the “oxygen catastrophe” of about 2.4 billion years ago also known?
100386.e: In scientific literature the event is called the Great Oxidation Event, GOE for short. The name “oxygen catastrophe” stresses that the new oxygen was devastating for many microbes of the time.
100386.m: The oxygen catastrophe is also called the Great Oxidation Event.

100387.q: Which protective layer of the atmosphere could only form after the rise in oxygen?
100387.e: Ozone forms from oxygen under UV radiation. Since then, the ozone layer has filtered out a large part of the harmful UV radiation.
100387.m: Without free oxygen there would be no ozone layer.

100388.q: Which sediments show from about 2.3 billion years ago that iron was also oxidising on land?
100388.e: The red colour comes from iron oxide such as haematite, which only forms with free oxygen. Such continental red sediments are missing in older layers.
100388.m: Red sandstones reveal oxygen in the atmosphere.

100389.q: What does the “Snowball Earth” hypothesis say?
a: The Earth was almost completely covered in ice over 600 million years ago
The Earth formed from a huge lump of ice
During the last ice age there was snow over the whole Earth
The Earth will freeze over completely in the future
100389.e: According to this hypothesis, the ice in the late Precambrian reached almost to the equator. Two such glaciations took place about 720 to 635 million years ago.
100389.m: Over 600 million years ago the Earth was probably almost entirely covered in ice.

100390.q: According to the Snowball hypothesis, roughly how many years ago was the Earth almost completely covered in ice?
100390.e: The great glaciations fall in the late Precambrian. They were therefore long before the dinosaurs and the last ice age.
100390.m: The Snowball glaciations were about 700 to 635 million years ago.

100391.q: According to the hypothesis, how did a Snowball glaciation end?
a: Volcanic carbon dioxide built up and warmed the Earth
An asteroid melted the ice suddenly
The Earth moved closer to the Sun
The continents drifted to the poles
100391.e: On a frozen Earth there is no weathering to bind carbon dioxide. But volcanoes kept releasing CO₂ until a strong greenhouse effect melted the ice.
100391.m: Volcanic CO₂ freed the Earth from its armour of ice.

100392.q: Which finding particularly supports an Earth almost completely covered in ice?
a: Glacial deposits that lay close to the equator at the time
Dinosaur bones in layers of ice
100392.e: Palaeomagnetic measurements show that some Cryogenian tillites formed at tropical latitudes. Glaciers at sea level at the equator point to a global glaciation.
100392.m: Traces of ice ages from the tropics support the Snowball hypothesis.

100393.q: Why was a Snowball glaciation so threatening for life in the sea?
a: The thick ice let hardly any light through for photosynthesis
The seawater turned into fresh water
There was no more oxygen in the air
100393.e: Algae and bacteria need light for photosynthesis. Under a closed sheet of ice, life could only survive in a few places, for example under thin ice or at hot springs.
100393.m: Without light under the ice, photosynthesis was hardly possible.

100394.q: Which feedback effect could have pushed the glaciation all the way to the equator?
100394.e: Ice reflects a lot of sunlight and so cools the Earth further. If the area of ice grows beyond a critical limit, the glaciation can reinforce itself.
100394.m: Bright ice cools the Earth and lets even more ice form.

100395.q: Which living things mainly existed at the time of the Snowball glaciations?
100395.e: About 700 million years ago, almost only single-celled organisms and simple multicellular ones lived in the sea. Larger animals and land plants only appeared later.
100395.m: At the time of Snowball Earth, mainly microorganisms lived.

100396.q: What does the opposing “Slushball Earth” hypothesis assume?
a: A strip of open water remained at the equator
The Earth was never colder than today
Only the continents were free of ice
The oceans were frozen to the bottom
100396.e: According to the Slushball hypothesis, the Earth was not completely frozen over. This would have made it easier for living things that carry out photosynthesis to survive.
100396.m: The Slushball hypothesis assumes open water at the equator.

a: A supercontinent about a billion years ago
An ancient ocean in the Mesozoic
A mountain range in present-day Russia
100397.e: Rodinia formed about 1.1 billion years ago and broke up from about 750 million years ago. Almost all the continental blocks of the time were united in it.
100397.m: Rodinia was a supercontinent of the Proterozoic.

100398.q: From which language does the name Rodinia come?
100398.e: The Russian word “rodina” means homeland or motherland. The name expresses the idea that all later continents came from Rodinia.
100398.m: In Russian, Rodinia means something like homeland.

100399.q: What formed when continents collided as they joined together to form Rodinia?
100399.e: When continents collide, rock is compressed and piled up into mountains. For Rodinia, the Grenville orogeny about a billion years ago was especially important.

100400.q: Which supercontinent already existed before Rodinia?
100400.e: Columbia, also called Nuna, existed about 1.8 to 1.5 billion years ago. Pangaea, Gondwana and Laurasia only formed much later, in the Phanerozoic.
100400.m: Before Rodinia there was the supercontinent Columbia.

100401.q: Which well-known supercontinent formed a few hundred million years after Rodinia broke up?
100401.e: Rodinia broke up from about 750 million years ago. About 300 million years ago the continents joined together again to form Pangaea.
100401.m: After Rodinia came the supercontinent Pangaea.

100402.q: According to most reconstructions, which continental core lay at the centre of Rodinia?
100402.e: Laurentia, the ancient core of North America, formed the centre of the supercontinent according to many models. The other blocks lay around it.
100402.m: At the centre of Rodinia lay the ancient continent of Laurentia.

100403.q: How could the break-up of Rodinia have encouraged the Snowball glaciations?
a: More coastline and rain increased the weathering that binds CO₂
The fragments blocked out the Sun
The break-up stopped all volcanic eruptions
100403.e: The break-up created many smaller, wetter land masses with long coastlines. More rain increased the weathering of silicate rock, which removes carbon dioxide from the air.
100403.m: The break-up of Rodinia may have cooled the Earth through weathering.

100404.q: What is the repeated formation and break-up of supercontinents called?
100404.e: In the supercontinent cycle, the continents join together roughly every few hundred million years and break apart again. Columbia, Rodinia and Pangaea are stages of this cycle.
100404.m: Supercontinents form and break up in a long cycle.

100405.q: How many major mass extinctions (the “Big Five”) are usually distinguished for the Phanerozoic?
100405.e: The Big Five came at the end of the Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic and Cretaceous. There were also many smaller extinction events.
100405.m: Five major mass extinctions are distinguished.

100406.q: Which of the five major mass extinctions is the oldest?
a: The one at the end of the Ordovician
The one at the end of the Cretaceous
The one at the end of the Triassic
The one at the end of the Permian
100406.e: About 444 million years ago many sea creatures disappeared. The main cause is thought to be a glaciation on the southern continent of Gondwana, with falling sea levels.
100406.m: The oldest of the major mass extinctions happened at the end of the Ordovician.

100407.q: Which habitats suffered especially badly in the mass extinction of the late Devonian?
100407.e: In the late Devonian, reef-building organisms and tropical sea creatures in particular died out. Water low in oxygen in the seas is considered an important cause.
100407.m: The Devonian mass extinction hit the reefs above all.

100408.q: Which event began about 201 million years ago and is regarded as the cause of the mass extinction at the end of the Triassic?
a: Huge volcanic eruptions as Pangaea broke up
An ice age at the equator
100408.e: As the Atlantic tore open, enormous amounts of lava poured out. Their gases greatly changed the climate and the chemistry of the oceans.
100408.m: At the end of the Triassic, volcanoes triggered a mass extinction as Pangaea broke up.

100409.q: How do researchers recognise a mass extinction in the Earth's history?
a: A great many fossil groups disappear from the layers within a short time
The rock layers suddenly become thicker
There are no rocks from this time
Fossils become larger at this time
100409.e: Palaeontologists count how many species or families appear for the last time in a period. If the extinction rate is far above normal, it is called a mass extinction.
100409.m: A mass extinction shows up as the sudden disappearance of many fossil groups.

100410.q: What typically follows a mass extinction?
a: An adaptive radiation of the surviving groups
The return of the extinct species
100410.e: Empty ecological niches are filled again by survivors, which split into many new species. This is how mammals spread after the end of the Cretaceous.
100410.m: After mass extinctions, survivors fill the empty niches.

100411.q: What is today's human-caused decline in biodiversity often called?
100411.e: Many experts see today's extinction rate as far above the natural background. The main causes are habitat destruction, overexploitation and climate change.
100411.m: Today's loss of species is often called the sixth mass extinction.

100412.q: What is the steady, normal extinction of individual species between the major events called?
100412.e: Even without catastrophes, species keep dying out, for example through competition or climate changes. It is only a mass extinction when the rate rises far above this.
100412.m: Background extinction is the normal loss of species in the Earth's history.

100413.q: Which volcanic province is regarded as the main cause of the mass extinction at the Permian-Triassic boundary?
100413.e: In Siberia, huge amounts of basalt lava poured out over a long time. Released gases such as carbon dioxide led to strong warming and changed the oceans.
100413.m: The Siberian Traps triggered the dying at the end of the Permian.

100414.q: According to common estimates, what share of marine animal species died out at the Permian-Triassic boundary?
100414.e: Estimates suggest about 90 per cent or more of marine species. On land, too, a large part of the vertebrate species died out.
100414.m: At the end of the Permian most sea life disappeared.

100415.q: What nickname is the mass extinction at the Permian-Triassic boundary known by?
100415.e: The name “The Great Dying” stresses the enormous scale of the event.
100415.m: The extinction at the end of the Permian is called the Great Dying.

100416.q: Which group of arthropods, which had existed since the Cambrian, finally disappeared at the Permian-Triassic boundary?
100416.e: Trilobites lived in the seas for about 270 million years. After declines in earlier crises, their last representatives died out at the end of the Permian.
100416.m: With the end of the Permian, the trilobites disappeared for ever.

100417.q: Which plant-eating animal with two tusks survived and was widespread in the early Triassic?
100417.e: Lystrosaurus belonged to the dicynodonts, relatives of the ancestors of mammals. Its fossils are common on several continents in the early Triassic.
100417.m: Lystrosaurus was a successful survivor of the end of the Permian.

100418.q: Which changes in the sea contributed greatly to the dying at the Permian-Triassic boundary?
a: Acidification, warming and lack of oxygen
The sea suddenly becoming fresh water
The salt content falling to zero
100418.e: A lot of dissolved carbon dioxide made the water more acidic and made it harder to build chalky shells. Warmer water also contains less oxygen, so zones low in oxygen spread.
100418.m: Acidic, warm and oxygen-poor seawater killed most sea creatures.

100419.q: Which two eras does the Permian-Triassic boundary separate?
100419.e: The Permian is the last period of the Palaeozoic, the Triassic the first of the Mesozoic. The boundary is also a break in the fossil record.
100419.m: The Permian-Triassic boundary separates the Palaeozoic from the Mesozoic.

100420.q: How can the Permian-Triassic boundary be recognised in rock layers all over the world?
a: By the sudden disappearance of many fossil species
By a thick layer of ice
By a layer of pure gold
100420.e: Below the boundary there are many species that are missing above it. Internationally, the boundary is defined in the Meishan section in China.
100420.m: The Permian-Triassic boundary shows up as a mass dying in the fossil record.

100421.q: Which researchers discovered a raised iridium content in the boundary layer in 1980 and interpreted it as a trace of an impact?
100421.e: The physicist Luis Alvarez and his son, the geologist Walter Alvarez, published the impact hypothesis in 1980. Iridium is rare in the Earth's crust but more common in asteroids.
100421.m: Father and son Alvarez founded the impact hypothesis.

100422.q: On which peninsula is the Chicxulub crater?
100422.e: The crater lies in the north of Yucatán in Mexico, partly under the Gulf of Mexico. It is buried under younger sediments and was proven with gravity and drilling data.
100422.m: The Chicxulub crater lies on Yucatán in Mexico.

100423.q: Roughly what is the diameter of the Chicxulub crater?
100423.e: The crater measures about 180 kilometres. The impacting body itself is estimated to have been about 10 to 15 kilometres across.
100423.m: The Chicxulub crater is about 180 kilometres wide.

100424.q: Roughly how many million years ago was the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary?
100424.e: The boundary is dated to about 66.0 million years ago. It ends the Mesozoic and begins the Cenozoic, the age of mammals.
100424.m: The Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary was about 66 million years ago.

100425.q: Which volcanic province in India was also active around the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary?
100425.e: Enormous amounts of basalt poured out in the Deccan Traps. Whether they helped to cause or worsened the extinction is still debated today.
100425.m: The Deccan Traps were active at the time of the end of the Cretaceous.

100426.q: Which mineral finding in the boundary layer proves an enormous impact?
100426.e: Shocked quartz shows fine deformation lamellae that only form under extremely high pressure. Such pressures occur in meteorite impacts and nuclear explosions.
100426.m: Shocked quartz is evidence of enormous impact pressure.

100427.q: What does the T stand for in the older term K-T boundary?
100427.e: K stands for the Cretaceous (from the German word Kreide) and T for Tertiary. Because the Tertiary is now divided into the Palaeogene and Neogene, it is called the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary.
100427.m: The former K-T boundary is now called the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary.

100428.q: Which sea creatures with chambered spiral shells died out at the Cretaceous-Palaeogene boundary?
100428.e: The ammonites disappeared completely after more than 300 million years. Their relatives, the nautiloids, have survived until today.
100428.m: With the end of the Cretaceous, the ammonites died out.

100429.q: Why is a raised iridium concentration in the boundary layer considered evidence of an asteroid impact?
a: Iridium is more common in asteroids than in the Earth's crust
Iridium only forms in forest fires
100429.e: Iridium is very rare in the Earth's crust because it sank into the Earth's core with the iron. Stony meteorites contain much more of it, and an impact spreads it around the world.
100429.m: Iridium in the boundary layer reveals an impact from space.

a: In the Atlas Mountains in Morocco
100430.e: The site is in Yoho National Park in British Columbia. It is part of the Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks World Heritage Site.
100430.m: The Burgess Shale is in the Rocky Mountains in Canada.

100431.q: How did the marine fossils of the Burgess Shale end up at a height of over 2000 m in the Rocky Mountains?
a: Through glaciers that carried them up
Sea level used to be 2000 m higher
100431.e: The animals lived on the bottom of a sea in the Cambrian. During mountain building the layers were raised, and Charles Walcott discovered them high up in the Rocky Mountains in 1909.
100431.m: Marine fossils in the mountains show the uplift of the Earth's crust.

100432.q: Roughly how old are the fossils of the Burgess Shale?
100432.e: The Burgess Shale comes from the middle Cambrian. It is therefore slightly younger than the early Cambrian fauna of Chengjiang.
100432.m: The Burgess Shale is about half a billion years old.

100433.q: What makes the Burgess Shale so valuable for palaeontology?
a: It also preserves the soft parts of animals
It is made of pure amber
100433.e: Mudflows buried the animals quickly, cut off from the air. As a result, even muscles, gills and guts, which normally rot, were preserved.
100433.m: In the Burgess Shale even soft body parts are preserved.

100434.q: What do strange animals in the Burgess Shale, such as Opabinia with five eyes, show?
a: That a great many body plans arose quickly in the Cambrian
That there were already dinosaurs in the Cambrian
That animals lived on land at that time
That all animals looked the same at that time
100434.e: This is called the Cambrian explosion: within a few million years almost all of today's animal phyla appeared. Some forms, such as Opabinia, look like no animal living today.
100434.m: The Burgess Shale is a window into the Cambrian explosion.

100435.q: Which animal from the Burgess Shale was first reconstructed upside down and back to front?
100435.e: At first, the spines were thought to be legs and the legs to be tentacles on its back. Later finds showed the correct position, and Hallucigenia is now regarded as a relative of the velvet worms.
100435.m: Hallucigenia was at first reconstructed the wrong way up.

100436.q: Why is the small animal Pikaia from the Burgess Shale important for the history of vertebrates?
a: It had a notochord, a forerunner of the backbone
It was the first fish with jaws
It was the first land animal
It had a skeleton made of bone
100436.e: Pikaia had a flexible rod along its back and muscular body segments. It shows that the line of chordates, to which humans also belong, already existed in the Cambrian.
100436.m: Pikaia is one of the earliest known chordates.

100437.q: Which palaeontologist made the Burgess Shale world-famous with the book “Wonderful Life” (1989)?
100437.e: Gould interpreted the strange Burgess animals as a sign of how much chance shapes evolution. In German the book was published as “Zufall Mensch”.
100437.m: Stephen Jay Gould made the Burgess fauna popular.

100438.q: Which atmospheric chemist made the term Anthropocene well known from the year 2000?
100438.e: Together with Eugene Stoermer, Paul Crutzen suggested regarding the present as a separate epoch of the Earth's history. He argued that humans had become a geological force.
100438.m: Paul Crutzen shaped the idea of the Anthropocene.

100439.q: What did Paul Crutzen receive the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for in 1995?
100439.e: Crutzen, Mario Molina and Sherwood Rowland showed how nitrogen oxides and CFCs damage the ozone layer. Their work led to the ban on CFCs.
100439.m: Crutzen was honoured for his ozone research.

100440.q: In March 2024, how did the responsible subcommission of the International Union of Geological Sciences decide on the Anthropocene as an epoch?
a: It rejected it as an official epoch
It introduced it as an epoch straight away
It used it to replace the Pleistocene
It moved it to the Middle Ages
100440.e: The Subcommission on Quaternary Stratigraphy voted against the proposal for an Anthropocene epoch. Officially we still live in the Holocene, but the term remains widely used in science.
100440.m: So far the Anthropocene is not an official geological epoch.

100441.q: Why are lakes with undisturbed annual layers in their mud well suited to proving the start of the Anthropocene?
a: Human traces in them can be dated to the exact year
They contain especially many dinosaur bones
100441.e: In Crawford Lake in Canada, a separate layer is deposited every year. Traces such as plutonium from nuclear tests can be assigned to a particular year, which is why the lake was proposed as the reference section.
100441.m: Lakes with annual layers are a precise archive of human traces.

100442.q: Which signal was proposed as the worldwide start marker of the Anthropocene around 1950?
a: Plutonium from above-ground nuclear weapons tests
100442.e: The nuclear tests of the 1950s spread radioactive substances over the whole Earth. This trace can be measured at the same time in sediments and ice worldwide.
100442.m: Plutonium from nuclear tests was meant to mark the start of the Anthropocene.

100443.q: In which geological epoch do we live according to the official timescale?
100443.e: The Holocene began about 11,700 years ago after the last glacial period. It is the official current epoch as long as no Anthropocene is recognised.
100443.m: Officially we live in the Holocene.

100444.q: What is the sharp rise in population, energy use and environmental pressure since about 1950 called?
100444.e: The term Great Acceleration describes how many curves of the economy and the Earth system rise steeply after 1950. That is why 1950 was proposed as the start of the Anthropocene.
100444.m: Since 1950 people have spoken of the Great Acceleration.

100445.q: Which materials are regarded as typical new deposits of the Anthropocene?
100445.e: Such materials hardly occur in nature, or not at all, and are now found in young sediments. They are also called technofossils.
100445.m: Plastic and concrete are becoming traces of humans in rock.

a: A layered limestone structure made by microbial mats
100446.e: Stromatolites form when microbial mats, mainly of cyanobacteria, trap sediment and precipitate lime. Layer by layer, a lumpy or column-shaped structure grows.
100446.m: Stromatolites are stone structures built by microbes.

100447.q: Where do especially well-known living stromatolites grow today?
a: In Shark Bay in Western Australia
100447.e: In Hamelin Pool in Shark Bay the water is very salty. Many animals that graze on microbial mats are missing there, so stromatolites can grow.
100447.m: Stromatolites still grow in Shark Bay today.

100448.q: Why are stromatolites much rarer today than in the Precambrian?
a: Animals graze on the microbial mats
The sea is too cold for microbes today
There is no more sunlight in the sea
100448.e: With the arrival of animals such as snails, microbial mats were grazed and disturbed. In addition, other organisms pushed the mats out of many habitats.
100448.m: Grazing animals pushed out most stromatolites.

100449.q: Roughly how old are the oldest widely accepted stromatolites?
100449.e: Stromatolites from the Pilbara region in Western Australia are about 3.5 billion years old. They are among the oldest traces of life of all.
100449.m: Stromatolites are among the oldest traces of life on Earth.

100450.q: Why do stromatolites grow upwards in layers?
a: The microbes grow towards the light over trapped sediment
Waves stack shells on top of each other
100450.e: Photosynthetic bacteria need light. When sediment covers them, they move upwards and form a new mat, so layer after layer builds up.
100450.m: Stromatolites grow layer by layer towards the light.

100451.q: What does the word part ‘lite’ (from Greek ‘lithos’) in stromatolite mean?
100451.e: The name comes from Greek: ‘stroma’ means cover or bed, ‘lithos’ means stone. A stromatolite is therefore a ‘layered stone’.

100452.q: In which period of Earth’s history were stromatolites most widespread?
a: In the Precambrian, more than 540 million years ago
In the Cretaceous, at the time of the dinosaurs
In the ice age of the last 2 million years
100452.e: In the Precambrian there were hardly any animals that could graze on microbial mats. Stromatolites therefore covered large shallow seas.
100452.m: The heyday of stromatolites was in the Precambrian.

100453.e: Cyanobacteria form mats that trap sediment and precipitate lime. They carry out photosynthesis and brought oxygen into the atmosphere early on.
100453.m: Stromatolites are built mainly by cyanobacteria.

100454.q: Which features make a fossil a good index fossil?
a: A short lifespan of the species and a wide distribution
A long lifespan of the species and rare occurrence
Large body length and life on land
100454.e: A species that existed only briefly pins down the time precisely. Wide distribution and abundance allow layers to be compared at places far apart.
100454.m: Good index fossils lived briefly, were common and widespread.

100455.q: Which extinct cephalopods with a bullet-shaped calcite rostrum, popularly called ‘thunderbolts’, serve as index fossils of the Jurassic and Cretaceous?
100455.e: Usually only the solid, pointed calcite rostrum of a belemnite is preserved. Their species changed quickly, which makes them useful time markers.
100455.m: Belemnites left behind the thunderbolts as index fossils.

100456.q: Which colony-forming marine animals are important index fossils of the Ordovician and Silurian?
100456.e: Graptolites drifted in the plankton and so spread across all oceans. Their species changed rapidly, which allows a fine division of time.
100456.m: Graptolites divide up the Ordovician and Silurian.

100457.q: Why are tiny microfossils particularly good index fossils?
a: They are very common, even in small rock samples
They are especially large and easy to see
They occur in only one single place
100457.e: A handful of rock can contain thousands of microfossils. This allows precise dating even in drill cores.
100457.m: Microfossils are common and practical index fossils.

100458.q: Which coin-shaped single-celled organisms are index fossils of the Eocene and also occur in limestones of the Swiss Alps?
100458.e: Nummulites are large foraminifera with a lens-shaped shell. The name comes from the Latin ‘nummulus’, little coin.
100458.m: Nummulites are the coin stones of the Eocene.

100459.q: Which English geologist realised around 1800 that rock layers can be compared by their fossils?
100459.e: William Smith formulated the principle of faunal succession. In 1815 he published the first geological map of the whole of England and Wales.
100459.m: William Smith discovered the order of fossils in the layers.

100460.q: What is the method of dating rock layers using fossils called?
100460.e: Biostratigraphy uses index fossils to divide layers into zones. Radiometry, by contrast, measures the decay of radioactive isotopes.
100460.m: Biostratigraphy dates layers by their fossils.

100461.q: What kind of age does an index fossil on its own provide?
a: The exact date of the animal’s death
100461.e: An index fossil shows whether a layer is older, younger or the same age as another. Figures in years only come from combining it with radiometric dating.
100461.m: Index fossils give a relative age.

100462.q: What is a galvanic cell called that can be recharged by applying an external voltage?
100462.e: In a rechargeable battery (secondary cell), the cell reaction is reversible. During charging, it runs in the opposite direction as an electrolysis.
100462.m: An accumulator is a rechargeable galvanic cell.

100463.q: What is the polarity of the anode in a galvanic cell?
100463.e: Electrons are released at the anode and build up there. That is why it is the negative terminal in a galvanic cell.
100463.m: In a galvanic cell, the anode is the negative terminal.

100464.q: What is the job of the salt bridge in a galvanic cell?
100464.e: Ions move through the salt bridge and balance the excess charges in the half-cells. Without it, the current would stop at once.
100464.m: The salt bridge completes the circuit through moving ions.

100465.q: What is the galvanic cell made of a zinc half-cell in zinc sulphate solution and a copper half-cell in copper sulphate solution called?
100465.e: John Frederic Daniell developed this cell in 1836. It is the classic school example of a galvanic cell.
100465.m: The Daniell cell combines a zinc and a copper half-cell.

100466.q: What is the nominal voltage of an AA alkaline manganese battery?
100466.e: The cell of zinc and manganese dioxide in potassium hydroxide solution gives a nominal voltage of 1.5 V. Rechargeable NiMH cells of the same size give only about 1.2 V.
100466.m: An alkaline manganese cell gives 1.5 volts.

100467.q: Who built the first battery around 1800 from stacked zinc and copper discs with soaked cardboard?
100467.e: Alessandro Volta presented the voltaic pile in 1800. The unit volt is named after him.
100467.m: The voltaic pile is considered the world's first battery.

100468.q: Which energy conversion takes place in a galvanic cell?
100468.e: A spontaneous redox reaction is split in space so that the electrons flow through an external conductor. In this way, chemical energy is converted directly into electrical energy.
100468.m: A galvanic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy.

100469.q: In which direction do the electrons flow in the external wire of a Daniell cell?
a: From the zinc to the copper
From the copper to the zinc
They do not flow at all
100469.e: Zinc is less noble and gives up electrons. These flow through the wire to the copper electrode, where copper ions are reduced.
100469.m: In the wire, electrons flow from the less noble to the more noble metal.

100470.q: Which of these metals is the least noble, that is, has the most negative standard potential?
100470.e: At about -3.04 V, lithium has one of the most negative standard potentials of all elements. It gives up its electrons particularly easily.
100470.m: Lithium is one of the least noble metals of all.

100471.q: What do you see when you dip a shiny iron nail into copper sulphate solution?
a: Copper is deposited on the nail
Iron is deposited on the nail
100471.e: Iron is less noble than copper and gives electrons to the copper ions. The iron dissolves and reddish-brown copper coats the nail.
100471.m: A less noble metal reduces the ions of a more noble metal.

100472.q: Which of these metals dissolves in dilute hydrochloric acid, giving off hydrogen?
100472.e: Only metals with a negative standard potential can reduce oxonium ions to hydrogen. Magnesium is base, while copper, silver and gold are noble.
100472.m: Base metals dissolve in non-oxidising acids and form hydrogen.

100473.q: How can you recognise a noble metal in the electrochemical series?
100473.e: Noble metals have a higher standard potential than hydrogen, so a positive one. They give up electrons only with difficulty.
100473.m: Noble metals have a positive standard potential.

100474.q: Which of these metals has the highest standard potential?
100474.e: The redox pair Au³⁺/Au has a standard potential of about +1.5 V, higher than platinum, silver and copper. That is why gold is particularly resistant to corrosion.
100474.m: Among common metals, gold has the highest standard potential.

100475.q: Which element is the strongest oxidising agent in the electrochemical series?
100475.e: At about +2.87 V, the redox pair F₂/F⁻ has the highest standard potential. Fluorine therefore takes up electrons most strongly.
100475.m: Fluorine is the strongest elemental oxidising agent.

100476.q: What forms when chlorine water is added to a potassium bromide solution?
100476.e: Chlorine has a higher standard potential than bromine and oxidises bromide ions to bromine. The solution turns yellowish brown.
100476.m: A lighter halogen oxidises the ions of heavier halogens.

100477.q: What happens when you place a sheet of silver in copper sulphate solution?
100477.e: Silver is more noble than copper and cannot give electrons to copper ions. So no redox reaction takes place.
100477.m: A noble metal does not reduce the ions of a less noble metal.

100478.q: What does a strongly negative standard potential tell you about a metal?
a: It is a strong reducing agent
It is a strong oxidising agent
100478.e: A strongly negative standard potential means that the metal gives up its electrons very easily. This lets it reduce many other substances.
100478.m: The more negative the standard potential, the more strongly the metal reduces.

100479.q: Which ion concentration applies when measuring a standard electrode potential?
100479.e: Standard conditions include a concentration of 1 mol/L, 25 °C and about 1 bar pressure for gases. Other concentrations shift the potential.
100479.m: Standard potentials apply to concentrations of 1 mole per litre.

100480.q: Zinc has a standard potential of -0.76 V. What does this mean compared with the hydrogen electrode?
a: Zinc gives up electrons more easily than hydrogen
Zinc takes up electrons more easily than hydrogen
Zinc is more noble than hydrogen
100480.e: A negative standard potential marks a base metal. That is why zinc dissolves in hydrochloric acid, forming hydrogen.
100480.m: A negative standard potential marks a base metal.

100481.q: Copper has a standard potential of +0.34 V. What happens when you put copper in dilute hydrochloric acid?
100481.e: Copper is more noble than hydrogen and cannot reduce the oxonium ions of the acid. So no hydrogen forms and the copper stays intact.
100481.m: Metals with a positive standard potential are not attacked by dilute hydrochloric acid.

100482.q: What voltage does a cell made of magnesium (E° = -2.37 V) and silver (E° = +0.80 V) give under standard conditions?
100482.e: The cell voltage is E°(cathode) minus E°(anode). So 0.80 V minus (-2.37 V) = 3.17 V.
100482.m: The cell voltage is the difference between the two standard potentials.

100483.q: What voltage does a cell made of aluminium (E° = -1.66 V) and iron (E° = -0.44 V) give under standard conditions?
100483.e: Iron is more noble and forms the cathode. So -0.44 V minus (-1.66 V) = 1.22 V.
100483.m: A voltage also arises between two base metals.

100484.q: What material is the electrode of the standard hydrogen electrode made of?
100484.e: Platinum coated with finely divided platinum black catalyses the setting up of equilibrium between hydrogen gas and oxonium ions. It does not react itself.
100484.m: The hydrogen electrode needs a platinised platinum electrode.

100485.q: A galvanic cell has a positive cell voltage. What does this tell you about the reaction in the cell?
a: It constantly needs energy from outside
100485.e: A positive cell voltage corresponds to a negative Gibbs free energy of reaction. So the reaction supplies electrical energy by itself.
100485.m: A positive cell voltage shows a spontaneous reaction.

100486.q: Which chemist set up the equation for how electrode potentials depend on concentration in 1889?
100486.e: Walther Nernst formulated the equation named after him in 1889. He received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1920.
100486.m: The Nernst equation describes how the potential depends on concentration.

100487.q: At 25 °C, how does the potential of a half-cell with z = 1 change when the ion concentration falls to a tenth?
100487.e: At 25 °C, E = E° + (0.059 V/z)·lg(c). A tenth of the concentration means lg = -1, so a decrease of 0.059 V.
100487.m: With z equal to 1, the potential changes by about 59 millivolts per power of ten.

100488.q: What is the potential of a silver half-cell (E° = +0.80 V) at c(Ag⁺) = 0.01 mol/L and 25 °C?
100488.e: E = 0.80 V + 0.059 V·lg(0.01) = 0.80 V minus 0.118 V. This gives about +0.68 V.
100488.m: A lower ion concentration lowers the potential of a metal half-cell.

100489.q: At 25 °C, what voltage does a concentration cell made of two silver half-cells with 1 mol/L and 0.001 mol/L silver ions give?
100489.e: The difference in concentration is three powers of ten. With z = 1, ΔE = 3·0.059 V, so about 0.18 V.
100489.m: Even identical half-cells give a voltage if their concentrations differ.

100490.q: What is the potential of a hydrogen electrode at pH 7, 25 °C and 1 bar of hydrogen?
100490.e: For the hydrogen electrode, E = -0.059 V·pH. At pH 7 this gives about -0.41 V.
100490.m: The potential of the hydrogen electrode falls as the pH rises.

100491.q: Besides the gas constant R, which constant appears in the factor RT/(zF) of the Nernst equation?
100491.e: F is the Faraday constant, the charge of one mole of electrons. Together with R, T and z it forms the factor.
100491.m: The factor in the Nernst equation contains the gas constant, the temperature and the Faraday constant.

100492.q: What happens to the factor RT/(zF) when the temperature rises?
100492.e: The temperature T is in the numerator of the fraction. At a higher temperature, a change in concentration therefore has a bigger effect on the potential.
100492.m: At higher temperatures the potential depends more strongly on concentration.

100493.q: Which half-cell forms the anode in a concentration cell?
a: The one with the lower concentration
The one with the higher concentration
100493.e: The potential is lower in the dilute half-cell, so metal dissolves there. In this way the concentrations gradually even out.
100493.m: In a concentration cell, the dilute half-cell is oxidised.

100494.q: What is the potential of a nickel half-cell (E° = -0.25 V) at c(Ni²⁺) = 0.01 mol/L and 25 °C?
100494.m: For ions with a charge of two, the change in potential per power of ten is only half as large.

100495.q: Who received the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing the lithium-ion battery?
100495.e: John B. Goodenough, M. Stanley Whittingham and Akira Yoshino were honoured in 2019. At 97, Goodenough was the oldest Nobel Prize winner up to then.
100495.m: The 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry honoured the inventors of the lithium-ion battery.

100496.q: What material is the negative electrode of most lithium-ion batteries made of?
100496.e: Lithium ions can be stored between the layers of graphite during charging. Graphite is light, cheap and conducts well.
100496.m: The negative electrode of lithium-ion batteries is usually made of graphite.

100497.q: Which cathode material for lithium-ion batteries is considered particularly safe and needs no cobalt?
100497.e: Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is very stable when heated and contains no cobalt. That is why it is increasingly used in electric cars and home storage systems.
100497.m: LFP batteries are particularly safe and need no cobalt.

100498.q: What is the nominal voltage of a typical lithium-ion cell with graphite and lithium cobalt oxide?
100498.e: The nominal voltage is typically 3.6 to 3.7 V. That is much more than nickel metal hydride or alkaline cells.
100498.m: A lithium-ion cell gives about 3.6 volts.

100499.q: Which company brought the first commercial lithium-ion battery onto the market in 1991?
100499.e: Sony sold the first lithium-ion batteries in 1991, at first for video cameras. This began their triumph in portable devices.
100499.m: Lithium-ion batteries have been on sale since 1991.

100500.q: What is the storing of lithium ions between the layers of graphite called?
100500.e: In intercalation, guest particles slip between the layers of a host lattice without destroying its structure. This lets lithium ions move back and forth during charging and discharging.
100500.m: During charging, lithium ions are intercalated into the graphite lattice.

100501.q: Why do lithium-ion batteries not contain a water-based electrolyte?
a: Water would break down at the high cell voltage
100501.e: The cell voltage is far above the decomposition voltage of water, and lithium also reacts with water. That is why lithium salts in organic solvents are used.
100501.m: Lithium-ion batteries need an organic, water-free electrolyte.

100502.q: What is the self-reinforcing overheating of a damaged lithium-ion cell called?
100502.e: In thermal runaway, breakdown reactions produce more and more heat. The cell can catch fire or burst.
100502.m: A damaged lithium battery can catch fire through thermal runaway.

100503.q: Where do the lithium ions move when you charge a lithium-ion battery?
a: From the positive electrode into the graphite
From the graphite to the positive electrode
They stay still in the electrolyte
They leave the battery as a gas
100503.e: During charging, lithium ions from the metal oxide of the positive electrode are stored between the layers of graphite. During discharging they move back again.
100503.m: During charging, lithium ions move into the graphite electrode.

100504.q: Which chemist teaching in Basel discovered the principle of the fuel cell in 1838?
100504.e: Christian Friedrich Schönbein, professor at the University of Basel, described the effect in 1838. William Grove built the first fuel cell shortly afterwards.
100504.m: The principle of the fuel cell was discovered in Basel in 1838.

100505.q: Which product forms in a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell?
100505.e: Hydrogen and oxygen react to form water. The reaction energy is used directly as electrical energy.
100505.m: A hydrogen fuel cell produces electricity, heat and water.

100506.q: Which particles pass through the membrane of a PEM fuel cell?
100506.e: PEM stands for proton exchange membrane. The membrane only lets protons through, so the electrons have to take the external circuit.
100506.m: Protons pass through the PEM membrane from the anode to the cathode.

100507.q: What is the theoretical cell voltage of a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell at 25 °C?
100507.e: The voltage is the difference between the standard potentials of oxygen and hydrogen. In practice, a cell under load usually gives only 0.6 to 0.9 V.
100507.m: A hydrogen fuel cell theoretically gives 1.23 volts.

100508.q: Which precious metal is usually used as a catalyst in PEM fuel cells?
100508.e: Platinum speeds up the splitting of hydrogen and the reduction of oxygen. Because it is expensive, researchers are working on catalysts with less platinum.
100508.m: PEM fuel cells usually need platinum as a catalyst.

100509.q: Which substance is oxidised at the anode of a hydrogen fuel cell?
100509.e: At the anode, hydrogen gives up electrons and forms protons. At the cathode, oxygen is reduced.
100509.m: In a fuel cell, hydrogen is oxidised at the anode.

100510.q: Which type of fuel cell works with a ceramic electrolyte at temperatures above 600 °C?
100510.e: The SOFC uses an oxide ceramic that only conducts oxygen ions at high temperatures. In return, it can also use natural gas or biogas.
100510.m: Solid oxide fuel cells work at very high temperatures.

100511.q: Which type of fuel cell supplied electricity and drinking water on the Apollo moon missions?
100511.e: The Apollo spacecraft used alkaline fuel cells with potassium hydroxide solution as the electrolyte. The water produced served as drinking water for the crew.
100511.m: On the way to the Moon, alkaline fuel cells provided electricity and water.

100512.q: What fundamentally distinguishes a fuel cell from a battery?
100512.e: A battery contains its reactants from the start and eventually runs flat. A fuel cell supplies electricity as long as fuel and oxidising agent keep flowing in.
100512.m: A fuel cell works as long as fuel keeps being supplied.

a: A redox reaction forced by electric current
100513.e: In electrolysis, an external voltage forces a redox reaction that would not happen by itself. Electrical energy is converted into chemical energy.
100513.m: Electrolysis uses electrical energy to force a redox reaction.

100514.q: In which Swiss town did one of the first aluminium works in Europe start operating in 1888?
100514.e: The Aluminium-Industrie-Aktien-Gesellschaft (later Alusuisse) used the hydropower of the Rhine Falls in Neuhausen for molten salt electrolysis. Works in Valais were added later.
100514.m: The Swiss aluminium industry began at the Rhine Falls in 1888.

100515.q: Which three products does chlor-alkali electrolysis supply?
a: Chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide solution
100515.e: In the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution, chlorine forms at the anode and hydrogen at the cathode. Sodium hydroxide solution is left in the solution.
100515.m: Salt solution gives chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide solution.

100516.q: What is the voltage called that is needed in electrolysis on top of the theoretically calculated voltage?
100516.e: Because of hindrances at the electrodes, for example when gas forms, the calculated voltage is not enough. The overpotential depends strongly on the electrode material.
100516.m: Because of overpotential, electrolysis needs more voltage than calculated.

100517.q: What is the polarity of the cathode in electrolysis?
100517.e: In electrolysis, the cathode is connected to the negative terminal of the power source. Cations are reduced there.
100517.m: In electrolysis, the cathode is the negative terminal.

100518.q: In electrolytic copper refining, where do precious metals such as silver and gold collect?
100518.e: More noble metals are not oxidised at the anode and fall down as sludge. They are extracted profitably from this anode sludge.
100518.m: In copper refining, precious metals end up in the anode sludge.

100519.q: What is the electrolytic coating of an object with a layer of metal called?
100519.e: In electroplating, the object is the cathode, where metal ions from the solution are deposited. This is how parts are chrome-plated or gold-plated, for example.
100519.m: In electroplating, metal is deposited electrolytically on an object.

100520.q: Why is cryolite added in aluminium production?
100520.e: Pure aluminium oxide only melts at over 2000 °C. Dissolved in cryolite, molten salt electrolysis can take place at about 950 °C, which saves a lot of energy.
100520.m: Cryolite allows aluminium electrolysis at a lower temperature.

100521.q: Put simply, what is rust made of?
100521.e: Rust is a mixture of iron oxides and iron oxide hydroxides with varying water content. It is porous and does not protect the iron underneath.
100521.m: Rust is a porous layer of hydrated iron oxide.

100522.q: What is a short-circuited galvanic cell that causes corrosion on a metal surface called?
100522.e: When two different metals touch in the presence of an electrolyte, a local cell forms. The less noble metal dissolves.
100522.m: Local cells are tiny galvanic cells that destroy metal.

100523.q: Why do cars rust faster in winter on salted roads?
a: Salt lowers the temperature of the metal
100523.e: Dissolved road salt increases the electrical conductivity of water. This makes the electrochemical corrosion reactions run faster.
100523.m: Road salt speeds up corrosion because it makes water more conductive.

100524.q: What happens when a steel screw touches an aluminium sheet in damp conditions?
100524.e: Aluminium is less noble than iron and becomes the anode in contact corrosion. It therefore dissolves around the screw.
100524.m: In contact corrosion, the less noble metal dissolves.

100525.q: Why is aluminium resistant to corrosion in everyday life, even though it is a base metal?
a: It forms a dense oxide layer
It does not react with oxygen
100525.e: In air, aluminium immediately coats itself with a thin, dense layer of aluminium oxide. This passivation protects the metal underneath.
100525.m: A dense oxide layer passivates aluminium.

100526.q: Which alloying metal makes steel stainless?
100526.e: Above a certain chromium content, a thin, dense chromium oxide layer forms on the steel. It renews itself when scratched.
100526.m: Chromium protects stainless steel from rust with a dense oxide layer.

100527.q: What is the process called in which steel parts are dipped in molten zinc to protect them from corrosion?
100527.e: Hot-dip galvanising produces a firmly bonded zinc coating. Protected like this, crash barriers and masts last for decades.
100527.m: Hot-dip galvanised steel is protected from rust by a layer of zinc.

100528.q: Why does damaged tinplate rust especially fast at the scratch?
a: Tin is more noble than iron
Tin is less noble than iron
100528.e: Tinplate is tin-coated iron. If the tin layer is damaged, the less noble iron becomes the anode in the local cell and corrodes faster.
100528.m: A more noble protective layer only protects as long as it is undamaged.

100529.q: Which metal is suitable as a sacrificial anode for a steel ship's hull?
100529.e: A sacrificial anode must be less noble than the metal it protects. Zinc meets this condition, while copper, silver and lead are more noble than iron.
100529.m: Sacrificial anodes are made of a less noble metal than the protected part.

100530.q: Which household appliance often contains a magnesium sacrificial anode?
100530.e: Enamelled steel boilers are protected by a magnesium anode against corrosion at flaws in the enamel. It should be checked regularly.
100530.m: Many hot water boilers are protected by a magnesium anode.

100531.q: What is the protection principle called that the sacrificial anode belongs to?
100531.e: The protected metal is made the cathode, where no oxidation takes place. That is why it is called cathodic corrosion protection.
100531.m: A sacrificial anode makes the protected metal the cathode.

100532.q: Why does a sacrificial anode have to be replaced from time to time?
100532.e: The sacrificial anode is oxidised instead of the protected metal and dissolves. Once it is used up, the part itself starts to corrode.
100532.m: A sacrificial anode sacrifices itself and must therefore be renewed.

100533.q: What is cathodic protection called when a direct current source is used instead of a base metal?
100533.e: In impressed current protection, a power source pushes electrons into the part being protected. Pipelines and large steel structures are protected in this way, for example.
100533.m: In impressed current protection, a power source replaces the sacrificial anode.

100534.q: Which condition must be met between the sacrificial anode and the protected part?
a: They must be connected so that electricity can flow
They must be the same size
They must be made of the same metal
They must not be in the same water
100534.e: Electrons can only flow from the anode to the part through a conducting connection. Both must also be in the same electrolyte.
100534.m: The sacrificial anode and the part must be connected by a conductor.

100535.q: Why would copper be unsuitable as a sacrificial anode for an iron pipe?
a: Copper is more noble than iron
100535.e: Copper would become the cathode, and the iron would corrode even faster as the anode. A sacrificial anode must always be less noble.
100535.m: A more noble metal speeds up the corrosion of iron instead of preventing it.

100536.q: Where are sacrificial anodes typically fitted on ships?
a: On the hull below the waterline
100536.e: The steel needs protection where it is in the electrolyte, seawater. That is why the anodes are on the underwater part of the hull, often near the propeller too.
100536.m: Sacrificial anodes only work where they are in the water.

100537.q: At which university did Michael Grätzel develop the solar cell named after him?
100537.e: Michael Grätzel and Brian O'Regan presented the cell in 1991 at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Lausanne. It is a well-known Swiss invention.
100537.m: The Grätzel cell was invented at EPFL in Lausanne.

100538.q: What is the Grätzel cell also called?
100538.e: In the Grätzel cell, a dye absorbs the light and releases excited electrons. That is why it is called a dye-sensitised solar cell.
100538.m: The Grätzel cell is a dye-sensitised solar cell.

100539.q: Which nanoporous semiconductor takes up the electrons from the dye in the Grätzel cell?
100539.e: A porous layer of titanium dioxide nanoparticles offers a huge surface for the dye. It passes the electrons on to the electrode.
100539.m: In the Grätzel cell, titanium dioxide carries the electrons away.

100540.q: What happens to the dye in a Grätzel cell when light falls on it?
a: It is excited and releases an electron.
It takes up protons from the electrolyte.
It evaporates and has to be replaced.
It only turns the light into heat.
100540.e: The light lifts an electron in the dye to a higher energy level. This electron passes to the titanium dioxide and flows away as current.
100540.m: Light excites the dye to release an electron.

100541.q: Which natural process served as the model for the Grätzel cell?
100541.e: Like chlorophyll in plants, a dye captures the light. That is why it is also called artificial photosynthesis.
100541.m: The Grätzel cell copies the way plants collect light.

100542.q: What advantage does the Grätzel cell have over classic silicon cells?
a: It also works well in diffuse light
It has a much higher efficiency
100542.e: Grätzel cells also make good use of weak light and light falling at an angle, and they can be made coloured and translucent. However, their efficiency is usually lower.
100542.m: Grätzel cells also work in weak light.

100543.q: Thanks to their coloured, translucent design, what are Grätzel cells particularly suitable for?
a: as glass facades and windows on buildings
as a replacement for nuclear power stations
100543.e: Grätzel cells can be made coloured and partly transparent. The SwissTech Convention Center at EPFL in Lausanne has a facade made of such cells.
100543.m: Grätzel cells can be used as coloured glass facades.

100544.q: Why are Grätzel cells considered cheaper to make than classic solar cells?
a: They do not need high-purity silicon.
They are made almost entirely of gold.
100544.e: Silicon cells need extremely pure silicon, which takes a lot of energy to make. Grätzel cells use cheap substances such as titanium dioxide and are easier to manufacture.
100544.m: Grätzel cells do not need expensive ultra-pure silicon.

100545.q: Where is the energy stored in a redox flow cell?
100545.e: Two dissolved redox pairs are stored in separate tanks and pumped through the cell. So the energy is in the liquids.
100545.m: A redox flow battery stores energy in liquids.

100546.q: In the most common type of redox flow battery, which metal is dissolved in both electrolytes?
100546.e: The vanadium redox flow battery uses vanadium in different oxidation states. It is the most advanced type of flow battery.
100546.m: The best-known redox flow battery works with vanadium.

100547.q: Which special advantage characterises redox flow batteries?
a: Power and storage capacity can be scaled separately
They fit into any mobile phone
100547.e: The power depends on the size of the cell stack, the amount of energy on the size of the tanks. Both can be increased independently of each other.
100547.m: In flow batteries, the tanks determine the capacity and the cell stack the power.

100548.q: What separates the two electrolytes in the cell stack of a redox flow battery?
100548.e: The membrane stops the electrolytes from mixing but lets certain ions pass to balance the charge. It corresponds to the salt bridge of a galvanic cell.
100548.m: A membrane keeps the electrolytes of a flow battery apart.

100549.q: Why is it useful that both electrolytes of a vanadium flow battery contain the same element?
a: Crossing through the membrane does not ruin the electrolyte
It means no voltage is produced
100549.e: If ions pass through the membrane, only different oxidation states of the same element mix. The loss of capacity can then be fixed again by rebalancing.
100549.m: The same element on both sides makes the flow battery long-lasting.

100550.q: What are redox flow batteries mainly used for?
100550.e: Because of their low energy density, they are unsuitable for mobile devices. As large fixed storage systems, however, they can buffer electricity from sun and wind.
100550.m: Redox flow batteries are suitable as fixed grid storage.

100551.q: How do the electrolytes of a redox flow battery get into the cell stack?
a: They are filled in with spoons
They stay permanently in the stack
100551.e: Pumps move the electrolytes from the tanks past the electrodes and back. Running the pumps uses up part of the stored energy.
100551.m: Pumps keep the electrolytes of a flow battery moving.

100552.q: Why is vanadium particularly suitable for redox flow batteries?
a: It exists in several stable oxidation states
It is the lightest of all metals
It is the only metal that conducts electricity
100552.e: Vanadium can exist in solution in the oxidation states +2 to +5. This means both half-cells can run on the same element.
100552.m: Vanadium has several oxidation states and fills both sides of the flow battery.

100553.q: How long must a current of 5 A flow to transport 1 mol of electrons?
100553.e: t = Q/I = 96,485 C / 5 A ≈ 19,300 s. That is about 5.4 hours.
100553.m: The time is the charge divided by the current.

100554.q: How much copper (M = 63.55 g/mol) is deposited when a current of 2 A flows through copper sulphate solution for 1 hour?
100554.m: More current and more time deposit more copper.

100555.q: How much silver (M = 107.9 g/mol) does a current of 1 A deposit in 965 seconds?
100555.e: Q = 1 A · 965 s = 965 C, which is 0.01 mol of electrons. Silver ions have a charge of one, so 0.01 mol · 107.9 g/mol ≈ 1.08 g forms.
100555.m: A hundredth of a mole of electrons deposits a hundredth of a mole of silver.

100556.q: What does Faraday's second law state?
a: The same charge deposits amounts of substance in the ratio 1/z
The voltage is proportional to time
Gases only form at the anode
The mass does not depend on the charge
100556.e: If the same charge flows through different electrolytes, the deposited masses are in the ratio of their molar masses divided by the ion charge z. These are called equivalent masses.
100556.m: Equal charges deposit chemically equivalent amounts of substance.

100557.q: In which decade did Michael Faraday publish his laws of electrolysis?
100557.e: Faraday formulated the laws in 1833 and 1834. Terms such as electrode, anode, cathode and ion also come from him.
100557.m: Faraday laid the foundations of electrolysis in the 1830s.

100558.q: What charge is needed to deposit 1 mol of aluminium from Al³⁺ ions?
100558.e: Each aluminium ion needs three electrons. So Q = 3 · 96,485 C ≈ 289,500 C.
100558.m: Ions with a charge of three need three times the Faraday charge per mole.

100559.q: What charge is needed to produce 1 mol of hydrogen gas (H₂) by electrolysis?
